Generative grammar is a linguistic theory proposing that language is generated by a finite set of innate universal principles and rules operating on abstract structures. Developed by Noam Chomsky beginning in the nineteen-fifties, it revolutionized linguistics by shifting focus from describing observable patterns to explaining how the human mind produces and understands novel sentences. Generative grammar proposes that humans are born with an innate universal grammar comprising core principles shared by all human languages. It explains how speakers produce and understand infinite sentences using finite means, a property called the productivity of language. The theory distinguishes between deep structure, the abstract, underlying meaning, and surface structure, the actual sentence form, connected by transformational rules. It accounts for grammaticality judgments—the fact that speakers intuitively know what is or is not a grammatical sentence, without being taught explicit rules. Chomsky's Poverty of the Stimulus argument holds that children acquire language so quickly and accurately that they must have innate constraints on hypothesis space. Generative grammar rivals structural linguistics and behaviorism by rejecting the idea that language is simply learned through imitation and conditioning. Later developments include X-bar theory, Government and Binding, and Minimalism—increasingly abstract frameworks for syntax. These approaches transformed linguistics by moving away from strict behaviorism and structural methods. Behaviorist B.F. Skinner's account of language learning, which Chomsky famously rejected, exemplifies the theoretical gap that generative approaches addressed.
